readers.angle: FlowState (arXiv 2508.05287 v1-v3; OpenReview R50AT6nAsM, 9yNGBueKgZ) and its public code (granite-tsfm modeling_flowstate.py, HF ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-flowstate-r1 and ibm-research/flowstate), plus the prior work FlowState builds its sampling-rate mechanism on (S5, S4, HiPPO-LegS) and the model it takes CPM/missing-value handling from (TiRex).

papers.title: FlowState: Sampling Rate Invariant Time Series Forecasting (arXiv v1 7 Aug 2025; v2 19 Aug 2025, same text)
papers.arxiv_or_venue: arXiv 2508.05287v1/v2 (v2 differs from v1 only in the arXiv header line; I checked with a text diff)
papers.sections_read: All of v1 and v2 via arXiv HTML: Abstract; Introduction; Background (Time Series Forecasting; Models for time series data; Autoregressive Forecasting and MPI); FlowState (SSM Encoder Eq.1-2 + ZOH formulas; Functional Basis Decoder Eq.3-5; Adjusting Delta Eq.6; Parallel forecasts Eq.7; Causal normalization Eq.8-10); Experiments (Evaluation Setup, Metrics, Temporal Scaling, Context and Forecasting Length); Results Tables 1-3; Robustness to Unseen Sampling Rates (Fig.3); Ablation Table 4; Conclusion.
papers.mechanism: Encoder: a stack of N S5 layers. Each is a ZOH-discretized complex diagonal MIMO SSM (HiPPO init) followed by an MLP, with a skip connection. There is no patching. Decoder (FBD): the final encoder output at the last context step is read as coefficients of a Legendre basis. The resulting continuous function is sampled at spacing Delta. A single scale factor s_Delta multiplies Delta (Eq.6), which rediscretizes the SSM and rescales the decoder sampling. Training uses causal RevIN (running mean/std) and parallel forecasts from every prefix.
papers.input_reconstruction: Implicit ZOH only. The S5 ZOH formulas are applied to the raw samples on a uniform grid. There is no linear/spline reconstruction and no explicit continuous input path.
papers.where_nonlinearity_evaluated: At every observation (every sample index): the MLP after each S5 block, the residual/normalization, and causal RevIN (a per-step division by the running std). Background states that only the SSM output carries the nonlinearity.
papers.time_handling: Uniform grid. dt enters only as Delta*s_Delta (step-size rescaling) in the ZOH discretization and in the FBD output spacing. s_Delta is chosen from seasonality (s = 24/seasonality), not from the raw frequency. Effective context and horizon are L/s and T/s. No timestamps, no irregular dt.
papers.invariance_claim: Informal and empirical. The title says 'Sampling Rate Invariant'. The text says rescaling Delta gives 'similar representations, irrespective of the sampling rate'. There is no formal definition and no proof in v1/v2.
papers.grid_changes_tested: Real downsampling only. Loop Seattle, originally 5-min, is subsampled to 5..65 min in 5-min steps, target length 480, compared against TiRex, Chronos-bolt-b and Toto. The subsampling method (decimation or averaging) is not specified. Ablation 'w/o time-scale adjustment'. No knot refinement, no interpolation/upsampling, no missing-vs-rate separation, no irregular sampling.
evidence_quotes: Sec 'SSM Encoder': "One S5 layer l consists of an S5 block, followed by an MLP."
Sec 'SSM Encoder': "By supplying a different quantization parameter Delta, the SSM can produce similar representations, irrespective of the sampling rate."
Eq.(6): "Delta_bar = f(Delta, s_Delta) = s_Delta * Delta."
Sec 'SSM Encoder': "FlowState processes the time series as-is and does not perform any quantization or patching."

Sec 'Robustness to Unseen Sampling Rates': "Originally sampled at 5-minute intervals, we subsample the data to create versions with sampling intervals ranging from 5 to 65 minutes in 5-minute increments."
Background: "the state update of SSMs block is linear, and only the output of the SSM contains a nonlinear activation."
Sec 'Temporal Scaling': "we base this factor on seasonality rather than raw sampling frequency."
papers.reported_numbers: GIFT-ZS (79 tasks), MASE/CRPS: FlowState(T)-9.1M 0.719/0.489; FlowState(G)-9.1M 0.728/0.491; FlowState(T)-2.6M 0.731/0.498; TiRex 0.733/0.497. Chronos-ZS, MASE/WQL: FlowState(T)-9.1M 0.755/0.580. Ablation on FlowState(G)-2.6M: baseline 0.733/0.502; w/o time-scale adjustment 0.808/0.544; w/o parallel predictions 0.757/0.523. The Loop Seattle MAE is shown only as a figure. No HAR, EigenWorms, Speech Commands or PDM numbers.
papers.notes: v1/v2 are the same paper as the 9.1M/2.6M models (context 2048, decoder patch 24). The claim is weaker than v3: no equivariance proof, and only one scale factor (no separate s_E/s_F). The dt-only baseline in N2 is exactly what this paper does.

papers.title: FlowState: Sampling-Rate-Equivariant Time-Series Forecasting
papers.arxiv_or_venue: arXiv 2508.05287v3 (15 Jun 2026); ICML 2026, PMLR 306 (arXiv comment). ICML OpenReview id 9yNGBueKgZ (not accessible: 403 challenge)
papers.sections_read: arXiv v3 HTML: Abstract; 1 Introduction; 2 Background; 3.1 SSM Encoder (Eq.1-3, ZOH); 3.2 FBD (Eq.4-6); 3.3 Adjusting Delta (Eq.7); 4 Sampling-Rate Equivariance (Eq.8-12, Fig.2); 5 Parallel forecasts, 5.1 Causal normalization (Eq.13-16); 6 Experiments (6.1.x, 6.2 Table 1, 6.2.1 Fig.4, 6.2.2 Table 2 ablations); 7 Conclusion/Limitations; App A.1 (Table 3), A.2; App B.1 in full (Assumptions B.1-B.2, Prop B.3 with proof Eq.17-32, pointwise ops Eq.33-35, FBD Eq.36-38, end-to-end Eq.39-48, multi-layer remark Eq.49-54); B.2 (Fig.8); C.1-C.3; D.1 (time noise Eq.56, Table 7); D.2 (Algorithm 1), D.2.1-D.2.3; D.3 (Table 8); D.4.
papers.mechanism: Encoder: 6 layers. Each is an S5-like complex diagonal SSM with an output gate, h_t = c_t*sigmoid(W c_t + b) + D x_t (Eq.3), followed by an MLP and norm/residual. It is ZOH-discretized with a trainable per-state Delta_E in R^P. FBD: Legendre basis coefficients taken from the last encoder output and sampled at spacing Delta_F. There are separate scale factors s_E (encoder) and s_F (decoder), Eq.7. Setting s_E != s_F gives forecasts at a different rate than the input, e.g. an ETTh1 context producing an ETTm1-rate forecast.
papers.input_reconstruction: ZOH, stated explicitly (Eq.19: u~(t)=u(floor(t/Delta)Delta)). The linear SSM is solved exactly for this piecewise-constant reconstruction. The paper says the only approximation comes from the ZOH reconstruction. No linear-interpolation/FOH reconstruction.
papers.where_nonlinearity_evaluated: At every observation index: the output gate (sigmoid), the MLP, the residual and normalization, and causal RevIN. B.1 calls these 'pointwise operations ... act independently at each time step' and argues they add no temporal discretization error, only a Lipschitz amplification.
papers.time_handling: Step-size rescaling only: Delta_E -> s_E*Delta_E (all P per-state Deltas scaled by one scalar), and decoder spacing -> s_F*Delta. The grid is uniform with fixed dt per sequence. A selective (input-dependent) Delta_E was tried and hurt performance. The scale factor is set from seasonality (Algorithm 1) or from automatic seasonality detection (D.2.2). Decoder 'time noise' jitters the sampling locations during training.
papers.invariance_claim: Approximate sampling-rate equivariance. Eq.8: F_{Delta'}(x) ~ FBD_{Delta'}(SSM_Delta(x)). Prop B.3 bounds the gap between final states under two ZOH reconstructions of the same Lipschitz-M input by (||B||M/alpha)(1-e^{-alpha T}) max{Delta,Delta'}. Single-layer end-to-end: error <= C max{Delta,Delta'} (Eq.46-47). Multi-layer: only a recursion E_l <= L_l E_{l-1} + C_l max{Delta,Delta'} is sketched, under assumed Lipschitz inputs to each layer. The paper never claims exact invariance, and knot refinement is not a special case it discusses. Its bound gives a nonzero first-order error for a piecewise-linear path with slope M.
papers.grid_changes_tested: Real downsampling only. ETT1m (15-min) resampled to 15..135 min in 15-min steps, H=480, vs TiRex, TimesFM-2.5 and Chronos-2-Synth (Fig.4); the resampling method is not specified. ETTh1 context used to forecast at ETTm1 rate (Fig.2). Cosine-similarity maps of last-layer encodings, ETT1m (s=0.25) vs ETT1h (s=1), temporally aligned vs time-flipped (B.2 Fig.8). Scale-factor sweep on ETTm1 (D.2.3). Not tested: virtual-knot insertion, interpolation upsampling, random drop, irregular grids. Missing data: the pretraining series with many NaNs are split into shorter series (C.2). No knot-vs-measurement distinction.
evidence_quotes: App B.1: "The discretized SSM is by definition exactly equivalent to the sampled solution of the continuous-time system driven by u~(Delta) ... The only approximation relative to the original continuous signal u(t) comes from this ZOH reconstruction."

App B.1 'Pointwise operations': "These operations act independently at each time step and therefore do not introduce additional temporal discretization error. They may, however, amplify or attenuate the mismatch produced by the SSM state."
Prop B.3, Eq.(23): "||s(Delta)(T) - s(Delta')(T)|| <= (||B|| M / alpha)(1 - e^{-alpha T}) max{Delta, Delta'}."
Sec 4: "Therefore, FlowState is approximately sample-rate equivariant, with an approximation error vanishing as max{Delta,Delta'} -> 0."
Sec 4: "sampling the continuous input x at a different rate yields (approximately) the same latent state and thus the same continuous forecast, which can then be evaluated on any grid."

App B.1 multi-layer remark: "A full multi-layer proof requires tracking both the propagated mismatch from previous layers and the fresh ZOH discretization error introduced at each subsequent SSM layer."
Sec 3.1: "The SSM block is inspired by the S5, with an output gate for improved selectivity." and "Subsequently, the output of each SSM block is further processed by an MLP layer"
Sec 6.2.1: "Originally sampled at 15-minute intervals, we sample the data to create versions with sampling intervals ranging from 15 to 135 minutes in 15-minute increments."
App B.2: "This is only valid if the input context x_ETT1m and x_ETT1h are from the same underlying process, but just sampled with different rates."
Sec 6.2.2: "We found that for FlowState making Delta_E selective clearly decreases performance."
papers.reported_numbers: GIFT-Eval (97 tasks), MASE/CRPS: FlowState-18.6M 0.701/0.487; 10.6M 0.704/0.490; 3M 0.712/0.496; TimesFM-2.5 0.705/0.490; TiRex 0.716/0.488. Ablations on FlowState-3M (2k context): baseline 0.725/0.502 (+-7e-4/+-11e-4 over 3 seeds); w/o equivariance 0.799/0.553; w/o parallel forecasts 0.774/0.548; w/o output gate 0.726/0.505; S5 real 0.862/0.602; selective Delta_E 0.749/0.521; fixed linear decoder 0.754/0.526; Fourier 0.727/0.507; w/o time noise 0.740/0.518; w/o causal RevIN 0.738/0.513; automatic scale factor 0.746/0.521. Long-horizon benchmarks (A.1, averaged over H in {96,192,336,720}), MSE/MAE: ETTm1 0.346/0.354; ETTh1 0.393/0.403; Weather 0.211/0.236; Electricity 0.155/0.240. No HAR, EigenWorms, Speech Commands or PDM numbers.
papers.code_url_and_license: https://github.com/ibm-granite/granite-tsfm (Apache-2.0); HF ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-flowstate-r1 revision r1.1 (Apache-2.0) and ibm-research/flowstate r1.1 (research-use weights per the model card; HF tag says apache-2.0).
papers.notes: This is the closest prior work to N2 and must be cited. (i) It already defines sampling-rate equivariance of a continuous-time forecast and proves a first-order ZOH mismatch bound. Prop B.3 is a standard ZOH/variation-of-constants inequality and should be marked as existing. (ii) It explicitly argues that per-sample pointwise ops add no discretization error. This is exactly the claim N2's counterexample targets: in layers l>1 the SSM integrates a ZOH hold of a per-sample nonlinear sequence, so the gap is O(Delta), not zero. (iii) Its FBD already provides continuous-time output querying: forecasts can be sampled at any spacing via s_F. N2's output query rule must credit this. (iv) It has no FOH/exact-path integration, no fixed physical-time clock for the nonlinearities, no exactness claim, and no knot-vs-measurement distinction. Author name: IBM and NeurIPS pages list 'Thomas Bohnstingl' where arXiv lists 'Thomas Ortner'. Papers citing FlowState that I checked (TinyCast 2608.15767, Forecast Collapse 2608.14106, EXAONE Finance 2609.04239, Toto 2.0 2605.20119; abstracts only) do not address sampling-grid invariance.

papers.title: FlowState implementation: tsfm_public/models/flowstate/modeling_flowstate.py (granite-tsfm) + HF configs (ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-flowstate-r1, ibm-research/flowstate)
papers.arxiv_or_venue: GitHub ibm-granite/granite-tsfm (main; the gift-flowstate branch differs only in formatting); PyPI granite-tsfm 0.3.9 (its wheel's modeling_flowstate.py is byte-identical to main)
papers.sections_read: Read in full: modeling_flowstate.py (964 lines), configuration_flowstate.py, __init__.py, utils/utils.py (get_fixed_factor); HF config.json for the main (v1.0) and r1.1 revisions of both repos; both model cards; the getting-started notebook code cells. I also installed the package and ran it on CPU (see notes).
papers.mechanism: FlowStateModel.forward: (1) with_missing: NaN -> 0 plus a mask channel, so the input is [value, mask]; for MPI, mask_n all-masked steps are appended. (2) Causal RevIN: running mean/std over observed counts (cumsum), a per-step normalization. (3) Linear embedding 2->512. (4) Encoder, 6x FlowStateS5Layer: skip; S5Block (ZOH kernel, FFT convolution over the whole sequence, Re(C x), optional output gate sigmoid(Wy)*y, +D*u); MLP ('transformer' in r1.1: RMSNorm -> w3(silu(w1 x)*w2 x) + skip; 'gated' in v1.0: selu then x*sigmoid(Wx)); LayerNorm; residual. The last layer returns only positions from min_context-1 on. (5) FBD: Linear(512 -> 256 basis x 9 quantiles). Legendre basis of degree 255 (decoder_type 'legs'), evaluated at t_k = -1 + k*s*1.95/decoder_patch_len for k=1..int(decoder_patch_len/s) on the range [-1, 0.95], divided by 4. (6) De-normalize with the last-step RevIN statistics. FlowStateForPrediction stitches MPI patches, recomputes the quantiles, and returns the mean or median.
papers.input_reconstruction: None beyond an implicit ZOH. The kernel is exp(s*lambda*Delta*k) on a uniform index grid, with B_bar = (exp(s*lambda*Delta)-1)/lambda * B (exact ZOH). The time axis is the sample index only, with no timestamps.
papers.where_nonlinearity_evaluated: Per sample, in every layer: causal RevIN division (once, at input), output gate sigmoid (r1.1), SwiGLU with RMSNorm or selu*sigmoid (v1.0), and LayerNorm. All act on every time index of the input grid.
papers.time_handling: scale_factor s is a scalar per batch element. In the encoder it multiplies exp(log_Delta) (P=512 per-state Deltas per layer, initialised log-uniform in [1e-3, 1e-1]). lambda = -exp(log_Lambda_real) + i*Lambda_imag, B, C and D are unchanged. In the decoder it multiplies the basis sampling spacing and sets the patch length int(decoder_patch_len/s). In FlowStateForPrediction it sets the context truncation max_context = min(16384, int(context_length/s)) - mask_n. The FFT convolution needs a uniform grid, so there is no per-step dt and irregular sampling cannot be represented. Missing values are masked tokens on the same grid. get_fixed_factor maps a pandas freq string plus domain to s = 24/seasonality.
papers.invariance_claim: The code makes none. Docstrings describe scale_factor as adjusting 'Delta of the S5 block and the Functional Basis Decoder'. The model card says it moves to a 'timescale invariant coefficient space'.
papers.grid_changes_tested: The official notebook demonstrates decimation only: context[:, ::4] with scale_factor 24/6. No tests of interpolation or knot insertion.
evidence_quotes: get_discretized: "log_Lambda_bar = scale_factor.unsqueeze(1) * lambda_[None, None, :] * torch.exp(self.log_Delta)"
get_discretized: "B_bar = (1 / lambda_ * (kernel[:, -2] - 1.0))[..., None] * B_tilde"
FlowStateS5Block.forward: "xs = F.sigmoid(self.output_gate(xs)) * xs"
MLP.forward: "x = F.rms_norm(x, (self.dim,), self.rms_weight, 1e-6)" / "return self.w3(F.silu(self.w1(x)) * self.w2(x)) + skip"
FlowStateModel.forward: "mask = torch.where(time_first_past_values.isnan(), torch.ones_like(time_first_past_values), 0)"
FlowStateForPrediction.forward: "max_context = min(16 * 1024, int(self.config.context_length / scale_factor)) - mask_n"
FBD.get_t: "dt = scale * (self.range[1] - self.range[0]) / self.pred_dist" with "self.range = [-1.0, 0.95]"
getting-started notebook: "# We subsample the input, e.g., only consider every fourth step and then adjust the scaling factor accordingly."
papers.reported_numbers: My own CPU check (not from the paper). Setup: r1.1 granite weights; synthetic series of 1024 samples, sin(2 pi t/24) + 0.5 sin(2 pi t/168 + 0.3) + 0.1 N(0,1), s=1. Virtual-knot refinement: np.interp onto a grid r times finer, with s/r, prediction_length H*r, compared at common physical times. r=2: cosine 0.908 and relative L2 difference 0.434 of the last-step backbone state; forecast relative L2 difference 3.2% (1 patch) and 2.1% (24-step MPI). r=4: cosine 0.815, relative difference 0.635; forecast 4.6% / 3.1%. Per-layer relative difference at the last context step for r=2: embedding after causal RevIN 0.78%; layer-0 SSM block (includes the output gate) 4.4%, layer-0 output 9.3%; layer-1 SSM 18%; layer-3 SSM 44%; last-layer SSM 19%. Repeating the same input gives a difference of exactly 0. CPU time: ~0.4 s at L=1024, ~1.5-2.3 s at L=4093. Parameter count: 18.52M (r1.1).
papers.code_url_and_license: https://github.com/ibm-granite/granite-tsfm/blob/main/tsfm_public/models/flowstate/modeling_flowstate.py, Apache-2.0. PyPI granite-tsfm 0.3.9 (Apache-2.0; Python >=3.11,<3.14; requires torch>=2.10,<2.12 and transformers[torch]>=4.57.6,<6). HF weights: ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-flowstate-r1 (Apache-2.0; main=v1.0 with 9.07M params, context 2048, patch 24, mlp 'gated', no out_gate; r1.1 with 18.5M params, context 4096, patch 6, mlp 'transformer', out_gating true). ibm-research/flowstate has the same configs; its card says research use only.
papers.notes: CPU recipe (checked on torch 2.14.0+cpu, transformers 5.17.0, granite-tsfm 0.3.9 installed with --no-deps plus datasets, pandas, scikit-learn, deprecated, einops; pip warns about the version pins but it runs). Normal install: pip install granite-tsfm==0.3.9. Code: from tsfm_public import FlowStateForPrediction; m = FlowStateForPrediction.from_pretrained('ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-flowstate-r1', revision='r1.1').eval() (drop revision for v1.0). x = torch.tensor(series, dtype=torch.float32).view(1, L, 1), shape (batch, seq_len, n_ch=1); NaN means missing. with torch.no_grad(): out = m(past_values=x, scale_factor=s, prediction_length=H, batch_first=True, prediction_type='median') ('mean' is the default). Outputs: out.prediction_outputs (batch, H, 1); out.quantile_outputs (batch, 9, H, 1); out.backbone_hidden_state (1+mask_n, batch, 512), where index 0 is the last real context step; out.hidden_states is the per-layer (L, batch, 512) outputs plus the decoder coefficients. prediction_length=-1 returns one patch of int(decoder_patch_len/s) steps with no MPI, which isolates the encoder. Longer H appends mask_n = H - int(patch/s) masked steps (CPM/MPI). For a knot-refinement test with factor r: pass the refined series with scale_factor=s/r and prediction_length=H*r, and compare refined forecast indices r-1::r with the original. Check that the refined length stays under min(16384, int(context_length*r/s)), otherwise the context is truncated and the physical window shrinks; the 16384 cap binds at r*... >= 4 for r1.1 at s=1. In FlowStateForPrediction scale_factor must be a Python float; per-sample tensors work only through FlowStateModel. The decoder casts its basis to float32, so a float64 reference would require editing get_kernel. The README's printed shape [32, 9, 48, 1] is stale; the actual output is (batch, 9, H, 1).

papers.title: Simplified State Space Layers for Sequence Modeling (S5)
papers.sections_read: Sec 3 (S5 layer, Eq.5-6 ZOH, timescale vector), Sec 3.3 parallel scans / irregular sampling paragraph, Sec 6.2 Speech Commands (Table 2), Sec 6.3 Variable Observation Interval (Table 3), App B.1.3 (timescale initialization), App D.5, App G activation description (weighted sigmoid gated unit), G.3.8 Pendulum.
papers.mechanism: A MIMO complex diagonal linear SSM, ZOH-discretized with learnable per-state timescales Delta in R^P and computed by parallel scan. A nonlinear activation is applied to the SSM outputs at each step; layers are stacked with norm/residual. FlowState's encoder is built on this.
papers.input_reconstruction: Implicit ZOH per step: Lambda_bar = e^{Lambda Delta}, B_bar = Lambda^{-1}(Lambda_bar - I)B. No linear/spline input reconstruction.
papers.where_nonlinearity_evaluated: At every observation/token: u'_k = GELU(y_k) * sigmoid(W GELU(y_k)), plus norms. For the pendulum task, a CNN encoder is applied per image and a per-step MLP decoder.
papers.time_handling: Two modes. (a) Global dt rescaling: Delta is multiplied by the ratio of sampling rates for 0-shot 16kHz->8kHz. (b) A variable per-step Delta_t supplied to the discretization for irregular observations (pendulum; the parallel scan allows a time-varying A_bar_k).
papers.invariance_claim: No formal invariance claim. It notes that continuous-time parameterisation lets the model be applied at other sampling rates 'without the need for re-training', and shows this empirically.
papers.grid_changes_tested: Real downsampling (naive decimation 16kHz->8kHz, 0-shot); irregular sampling (50 of 100 frames drawn without replacement, pendulum). No knot refinement, interpolation-based upsampling or knot-vs-measurement distinction.
evidence_quotes: Sec 6.2: "simply by globally re-scaling the timescale parameter Delta by the ratio between the new and old sampling rates."
Table 2 caption: "Last column indicates 0-shot testing at 8kHz (constructed by naive decimation)."
Sec 6.3: "S5 does so by supplying a different Delta_t value to the discretization at each step."
Sec 3: "A nonlinear activation function is then applied to produce a sequence of layer outputs u'_{1:L}"
App G: "the layer output of the activation function we apply is u'_k = GELU(y_k) (.) sigma(W * GELU(y_k))."
papers.reported_numbers: Speech Commands 35-way, raw 16kHz, test accuracy (mean of 3 seeds), 16kHz / 0-shot 8kHz by naive decimation with Delta rescaled: S5 96.52 / 94.53; S4-LegS 96.08 / 91.32; S4D-LegS 95.83 / 91.08; Liquid-S4 96.78 / 90.00; ConvNet 95.51 / 7.26; InceptionNet 61.24 / 5.18. Pendulum regression MSE x1e-3: S5 3.41 (0.27); CRU 4.63 (1.07); CRU (their run) 3.94 (0.21); ODE-RNN 7.26 (0.41); mTAND 65.64 (4.05).
papers.notes: This is the source of FlowState's scale mechanism and a standard reference for 'dt-only adjustment' and the Speech Commands 16k->8k resolution-change protocol. The 8kHz input is plain decimation with no anti-aliasing mentioned, so it is real downsampling, not lossless refinement.

papers.title: Efficiently Modeling Long Sequences with Structured State Spaces (S4)
papers.sections_read: Architecture paragraph in Sec 3 (H copies + position-wise mixing + nonlinearities), Sec 2.3 discretization sentence, Sec 4.2 Speech Commands (Fig.5/table), Sec 4.3 'Sampling resolution change'. Not read in full.
papers.mechanism: H independent SISO continuous-time SSMs (DPLR/HiPPO) discretized with a step size Delta and computed as a convolution. Layers alternate with position-wise linear mixing and nonlinear activations (GLU).
papers.input_reconstruction: None explicit. The discrete SSM (bilinear in the original S4) is applied to the samples.
papers.where_nonlinearity_evaluated: At every token/sample between layers (activation plus position-wise mixing).
papers.time_handling: Delta is a step size representing the input resolution. Resolution change is handled by changing the internal Delta at test time.
papers.invariance_claim: Empirical only: 'automatically adapts to data sampled at different rates'.
papers.grid_changes_tested: SC10 raw audio at 0.5x frequency at test time (downsampling, following the CKConv protocol). No knot refinement or interpolation test.
evidence_quotes: Sec 4.3: "Without re-training, S4 achieves 96.3% accuracy at 0.5x the frequency on Speech Commands 10 (Fig. 6), simply by changing its internal step size Delta (Section 2.3)."
Sec 3 architecture: "Nonlinear activation functions are also inserted between these layers."
Sec 2.3: "(1) must be discretized by a step size Delta that represents the resolution of the input."

readers.angle_summary:
FlowState (ICML 2026 as arXiv v3; a NeurIPS 2025 workshop version is OpenReview R50AT6nAsM) is the closest prior work in this angle, but it does not contain N2's central claim.

What FlowState does:
- **Encoder:** 6 S5-like complex diagonal SSM layers, ZOH-discretized with trainable per-state Delta_E. One scalar scale factor s multiplies all Deltas; A, B, C and D are unchanged.
- **Per-sample nonlinearities:** at every sample index there is causal RevIN, an output gate sigmoid(Wc)*c (r1.1), an MLP (SwiGLU+RMSNorm in r1.1, selu+sigmoid gate in v1.0), LayerNorm and a residual.
- **Decoder (FBD):** a Legendre ('legs') basis of degree 255 on [-1, 0.95], evaluated at spacing s*1.95/patch_len.
- **Grid and missing data:** the code uses an FFT convolution on a uniform grid. There are no timestamps and no per-step dt. Missing values become NaN masked tokens on the same grid (the TiRex style).
- **Formal claim (v3):** only approximate equivariance. Prop B.3 is a standard two-rate ZOH/variation-of-constants bound, O(M max{Delta, Delta'}). The multi-layer case is only sketched. The paper explicitly states that per-step pointwise ops 'do not introduce additional temporal discretization error'. That statement is exactly what N2's counterexample should target.
- **Experiments:** they test only real downsampling. Loop Seattle 5-65 min (v1/v2), ETTm1 15-135 min, ETTh1 context forecast at ETTm1 rate, encoder-correlation maps, and the notebook's [::4] decimation. They never test virtual-knot insertion, interpolation, random drop or irregular grids, and never distinguish knots from measurements.

Overlap with N2's four components:
- **Exact input integration:** partial. Exact ZOH solves the linear SSM exactly, but for a piecewise-constant reconstruction, not FOH.
- **Fixed-time nonlinearity:** none.
- **Refinement-invariance claim:** partial (approximate and first-order only).
- **Knot-vs-measurement distinction:** none.

What N2 must credit as existing:
- the notion of sampling-rate equivariance of a continuous-time forecast;
- dt-only rescaling (S4, S5, FlowState);
- ZOH mismatch bounds (FlowState Prop B.3);
- continuous-time output querying through a basis decoder (FBD, which also allows s_E != s_F);
- exact dilation equivariance of the continuous HiPPO-LegS operator (Prop 3), which is about dilation, not refinement.

S5, S4 and HiPPO all apply nonlinearities per step and test only decimation or timestamp scaling. Calibration numbers:
- Speech Commands 35-class, 16k to 0-shot 8k: S5 96.52 to 94.53.
- SC10 at 0.5x frequency: S4 98.32 to 96.30.
- Character Trajectories 100 to 200 Hz: HiPPO-LegS 88.8.
- None of these papers reports HAR, EigenWorms or PDM.

My own CPU check of FlowState r1.1 (not a paper result): refining a synthetic series by r=2 on its piecewise-linear interpolant, with s/2, left the forecast about 2-3% different at common times. The last-layer representation changed much more (cosine 0.908). The layer-wise difference grows with depth, from 0.8% after causal RevIN to 4-9% at layer 0 and roughly 40% at layers 3-4. This is a concrete counterexample on a real pretrained model, consistent with N2's hypothesis.

Access limits: all OpenReview pages (R50AT6nAsM, 9yNGBueKgZ, mkOc8O6Xxa) returned a 403 challenge, so the reviews were not read.

Files, all in the scratchpad /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Sampling-Consistent-State-Space-Models-with-Fixed-Time-Nonlinearities/433b875b-7be5-5546-a08e-fa52cd86113e/scratchpad/:
- fs_knot_test.py and fs_layerwise.py (the test scripts)
- venv_fs/ (a working CPU environment)
- fs/ (downloaded sources and text versions)

papers.title: Multirate State Space Models for End-to-End Processing of Pulse Density Modulated Speech Signals
papers.sections_read: Abstract; I Introduction; II-A PDM; II-B SSMs (Eqs 1-6); III-A SSM Encoder Layer (Figs 4-6); III-B Architecture (Fig 7); IV-A..IV-D (training, PDM evaluation, KWS and SE setups); V-A1..V-A3, V-B1..V-B3 (all results); VI Conclusion; references [1]-[38]
papers.mechanism: A fixed-structure continuous-time HiPPO SSM (LegT or FouT, dense A in R^{HxH}, memory window theta seconds) is discretized with the BILINEAR method at step Delta = 1/f_s of the incoming stream (16 kHz PCM or 128 kHz-2 MHz PDM bitstream) and run at the input rate. Its coefficient vector x[n] is then decimated to a FIXED output rate by keeping one vector every K_PDM = K_PCM x OSR samples (no anti-alias filter). All nonlinear processing (an S4D-style SSM stack with dense layers for KWS; LiSenNet for speech enhancement) runs only on this fixed-rate decimated sequence. For SE the predicted coefficients are projected back onto the basis at the PCM rate and overlap-added.
papers.input_reconstruction: None explicit. The bilinear rule (Eq. 2) is applied to raw samples (PCM values or +/-1 PDM bits). There is no ZOH or FOH closed-form integration of a reconstructed path. The test-set PDM signals are made by cubic-spline upsampling of PCM followed by a 2nd-order sigma-delta modulator.
papers.where_nonlinearity_evaluated: Only after the linear encoder, on the decimated fixed-rate grid n*K_PDM/f_PDM (= n*K_PCM/16 kHz), which is a fixed physical-time clock when OSR is an integer. The encoder itself is linear. The downstream KWS stack evaluates dense/pointwise nonlinearities at every decimated step.
papers.time_handling: Physical step size Delta = 1/f_s in the encoder (the only change between PCM and PDM is Delta). The decimation hop is tied to OSR (an integer), so encoder output times are aligned to a fixed physical rate. The downstream KWS SSMs have per-channel learnable Delta. Downstream rates as low as 31.25 Hz were used (K = 65,536 at 2 MHz).
papers.invariance_claim: The paper claims a 'modulation- and sampling-rate-invariant latent representation'. The claim is APPROXIMATE and EMPIRICAL: coefficient trajectories are 'nearly identical, up to the quantization noise' (Fig. 6, qualitative), and for integer K the decimated PDM coefficients 'encode the same continuous-time history' as the PCM ones. There is no exactness theorem, no error bound and no discretization-error analysis. Decimating below Nyquist 'without anti-aliasing' is justified by the overlapping memory windows and the low-pass spectra of the LegT/FouT bases, not by any guarantee.
papers.grid_changes_tested: Train on 16 kHz PCM, test on PDM at OSR 8-128 (128 kHz-2 MHz). This changes the modulation (1-bit quantized, noise-shaped) as well as the rate, so it is not a lossless knot refinement of the same path. Coefficient decimation factors K_PDM of 128-65,536 were also tested, i.e. real downsampling of the latent. Not tested: irregular grids, missing observations, non-integer rate ratios, or virtual-knot refinement.
evidence_quotes: Fig. 4: "it encodes the input data as a sequence of SSM coefficient vectors, then downsamples them from the variable-OSR PDM rate to a fixed rate by retaining one coefficient vector every $K=OSR$ time steps."
Sec. II-B (Eq. 2): "before being applied to a discrete-time (DT) signal, the $A$ and $B$ matrices need to be discretized by a step size $\Delta$ using techniques such as the bilinear method"

Sec. III-A: "The only difference between the two configurations is the discretization step, set to $\Delta=1/16{,}000$ for PCM and $\Delta=1/1{,}024{,}000$ for PDM. The resulting coefficient trajectories are nearly identical, up to the quantization noise"

Sec. III-A: "For integer $K_{\mathrm{PDM}}$ , the downsampled PDM coefficients $\mathbf{x}[nK_{\mathrm{PDM}}]$ encode the same continuous-time history as the corresponding PCM coefficients $\mathbf{x}[n]$ ."

Sec. I: "we show that this representation can be efficiently downsampled without anti-aliasing to a fixed-rate coefficient sequence, making the downstream layers agnostic to both the input modulation and sampling rate."

Sec. III-A: "If the PCM coefficients are downsampled by a factor $K_{PCM}$ , the PDM coefficients must be downsampled by $K_{PDM}=K_{PCM}\times OSR$ to keep the encoder output rate consistent across modulations."

Sec. IV-B: "we first interpolate the PCM data using a cubic spline interpolation with a specific OSR factor and use a single-bit second-order $\Sigma\Delta$ modulator to convert the interpolated PCM stream to a PDM stream."
papers.reported_numbers: KWS on Google Speech Commands (35 classes), trained on 16 kHz PCM with noise augmentation. Test on 2 MHz PDM (OSR 128) with K_PDM = 128: best LegT (H=128, theta=8 ms) 93.72%; best FouT (H=512, theta=32 ms) 93.44%. Lowest-cost LegT (H=32, theta=2 ms): 93.53% on PCM, >92% for PDM at 512 kHz and above, 92.66% at 512 kHz, 93.13% at 2 MHz (Conclusion). Decimation sweep at 2 MHz with theta_PDM = 16,384 samples (8 ms): 88% up to K = theta_PDM, 83% up to K = 4 theta_PDM, and a drop of less than 10% up to K = 65,536 (31.25 Hz downstream). The text says H=32 but the Fig. 9 caption says H is fixed at 128, an internal inconsistency. The authors note these numbers are below the ~96% of the S4D reference [31], which used more parameters and bidirectional layers. Speech enhancement on VoiceBank+DEMAND: FouT theta=32 ms, H=512 gives PESQ 3.24 and STOI 93% at 2 MHz. theta=2 ms, H=32 gives PESQ 3.08 and STOI 93%, versus PCM LiSenNet at 3.07 / 94%. Across PDM rates (FouT, 2 ms, H=32, 75% overlap): PESQ 2.24 at 128 kHz (noisy input 2.0), 2.98 / 0.92 at 512 kHz, 3.08 / 0.93 at 2 MHz.
papers.code_url_and_license: https://github.com/NECOTIS/ssm-speech-processing.git. The paper says the code 'will be made available'. The repo could not be checked from this session (GitHub API returned 403). License unknown.
papers.notes: This is the closest published precedent to N2's architecture: a linear continuous-time SSM integrates the high-rate input, is sampled on a fixed physical clock, and only then enter nonlinear layers. N2 therefore cannot claim the 'stem + fixed-clock decimation before nonlinearities' structure, or 'SSM-based rate-invariant multirate front end', as new. What still separates N2: (i) closed-form exact integration over an explicit FOH/piecewise-linear reconstruction, where this paper uses bilinear on raw samples; (ii) exact invariance to virtual-knot refinement as a theorem, where this paper has only empirical approximate similarity; (iii) arbitrary, non-integer or irregular grids with clock points tau_j falling between observations, where this paper has integer OSR and aligned hops; (iv) explicitly separating lossless refinement, real downsampling (aliasing) and missing data, none of which is separated here; (v) a learned diagonal stem rather than a fixed LegT/FouT. PDM-vs-PCM is not the same reconstructed path, so none of this paper's results is a refinement-invariance test. The text does not say whether the encoder A,B are trained. The reported 112k total parameters at H=512 is smaller than a dense 512x512 A, which suggests the encoder is not counted or not trained, but this is unconfirmed. Any N2 PDM experiment must include this architecture as a baseline, or the gain may be explained by it (NO_GO risk).

papers.title: Efficient and interpretable raw audio classification with diagonal state space models (S-Edge)
papers.arxiv_or_venue: Machine Learning (Springer) 114:175, published 19 Jun 2025 (ECML-PKDD 2025 journal track); no arXiv id found
papers.sections_read: Abstract; 1 Introduction; 2.1-2.3 Related work (Eqs 1-6); 3.1 S-Edge layer (Eqs 7-9); 3.2 Layer-wise downsampling and RZOH (Table 1, Fig 2); 3.3 Interpretability (Eqs 14-16); 4.1-4.3 Results (Tables 2-4); 5 Conclusion; App. A.1 RZOH, A.2 init/training, start of A.3
papers.mechanism: Stack of diagonal complex MIMO SSM layers (S5-like, ZOH, global sampling time Ts, learnable Delta) with Leaky-ReLU nonlinearities. It uses layer-wise downsampling: at inference, feature maps are naively decimated between layers (e.g. factors [1,1,1,2,2,38]), and each later layer is re-discretized with the new Ts, so deeper layers run at lower physical rates (16 kHz down to 421.05 Hz). RZOH regularization randomly downsamples and then ZOH-upsamples feature maps during training to expose the network to aliasing and discretization error.
papers.input_reconstruction: ZOH (Eq. 3/6) on raw 16 kHz audio. Between layers, decimation is naive (no anti-alias filter). RZOH upsamples by ZOH.
papers.where_nonlinearity_evaluated: At every sample of each layer's own grid. The first layers run at the input rate (16 kHz), deeper layers at their decimated rates. Nonlinearities are never evaluated on a clock independent of the input grid, since layer rates are integer divisions of the input rate.
papers.time_handling: Physical Ts plus a learnable per-state Delta, rescaled after each downsampling. A 16 kHz-trained model is evaluated on input decimated to 8 or 4 kHz by rescaling. Internal rates are chosen by brute-force search (6,686 configurations per 6-layer model).
papers.invariance_claim: None. The authors state explicitly that 16 kHz-trained networks lose accuracy at 8 kHz and that naive downsampling may alias. The goal is compute efficiency, not invariance.
papers.grid_changes_tested: Real downsampling of the input (16 to 8 to 4 kHz) and internal per-layer decimation (factors up to 64 per layer). No knot refinement, irregular or missing tests.
evidence_quotes: Sec. 1: "We apply a layer-wise downsampling to execute layers at different temporal resolutions. Specifically, we infer deeper layers with lower sampling rates (similar to a stride in the time domain)."
Sec. 3.2: "We use naive downsampling, as it is the computationally cheapest method, allowing for significant optimizations, although it may introduce aliasing errors."
Sec. 3.2: "When downsampling somewhere the sampling rate of all following layers has to be updated (see Fig. 2)."
Sec. 3.2: "Random Zero Order Hold (RZOH) introduces discretization/aliasing error during training to strengthen the network against it, by randomly first downsampling and then upsampling featuremaps"
Sec. 3.2: "All currently available tests show that NNs trained for 16kHz lose accuracy on 8kHz (Smith et al., 2023; Gu et al., 2024; Hasani et al., 2023)."
papers.reported_numbers: Speech Commands, 35 classes, raw audio, causal models (Table 2, input downsampling only): S5 (208k parameters, causal reproduction) 95.83% at 16 kHz / 93.53% at 8 kHz. S5-LeakyReLU (151k) 95.41 / 90.60. S-Edge-Full (141k) 95.19 / 93.38 / 81.11 at 4 kHz. S-Edge-Tiny (8k) 90.50 / 85.82 / 67.32. S4-LegS (306k) 93.60 at 16 kHz. With internal downsampling and RZOH (Table 3), S-Edge-Full scores 95.22 / 95.17 / 94.38 / 93.66 / 90.31 / 74.94 at >=1x/2x/4x/5x/8x/16x FLOP reduction; without RZOH, 94.92 / 93.39 / 85.14 / 82.64 / 65.63 / 23.58. On an ARM Cortex-M4F the largest model takes 103 s per inference at 95.19%, the smallest 0.29 s at 88.01%.
papers.code_url_and_license: https://github.com/embedded-machine-learning/S-Edge (plus a Cpp-NN repo). The paper says the code will be available after acceptance. License not checked.
papers.notes: A multirate deep SSM with physical-time rescaling per layer and the dt-only zero-shot 16-to-8 kHz baseline. Useful calibration for SC resolution change: dt rescaling alone costs about 2.3 points (S5, 16 to 8 kHz causal). Nonlinearities stay tied to the input grid, so this is not an N2-type fixed clock. RZOH is a training-time aliasing augmentation. N2 should not claim 'layer-wise multirate SSMs' as new.

papers.title: FlowState: Sampling-Rate-Equivariant Time-Series Forecasting
papers.arxiv_or_venue: arXiv 2508.05287v3 (15 Jun 2026); ICML 2026 poster (per icml.cc listing found by search)
papers.sections_read: Abstract; Sec 3.1 SSM encoder (S5 layers + MLP, ZOH Eq.); Sec 3.2 functional basis decoder; Sec 3.3 Adjusting Delta; Sec 4 Sampling-Rate Equivariance; App. B.1 formal analysis (Assumptions B.1-B.2, Prop. B.3, Eqs 17-54 including the multi-layer remark); start of App. B.2 empirical validation
papers.mechanism: An S5-based SSM encoder (diagonal, ZOH, trainable Delta_E) with an output gate, residual connections, normalization and an MLP after every SSM block. It feeds a Legendre functional-basis decoder whose continuous forecast is sampled at Delta_F. Unseen sampling rates are handled by scaling Delta: bar-Delta = s_Delta * Delta.
papers.input_reconstruction: ZOH (piecewise-constant) of the input samples, stated explicitly in App. B.1, Eq. 19.
papers.where_nonlinearity_evaluated: At every input time step (pointwise gate and MLP after each SSM layer). The decoder's nonlinear parts act on the final encoder state.
papers.time_handling: dt rescaling via a scale factor s_Delta (the step-size-rescaling family). Time noise is added in the decoder during training.
papers.invariance_claim: APPROXIMATE equivariance. Single-layer bound: ||s^Delta(T) - s^Delta'(T)|| <= (||B|| M / alpha)(1 - e^{-alpha T}) max{Delta, Delta'} (Prop. B.3). A multi-layer recursion E_l <= L_l E_{l-1} + C_l max{Delta, Delta'} gives O(max Delta) (Eqs 53-54). The paper asserts that pointwise operations add no discretization error. Empirically, encodings of ETT1m and ETT1h are correlated.
papers.grid_changes_tested: Real subsampling (ETT1m to ETT1h, i.e. 15-min to hourly) and unseen sampling rates on GIFT-Eval. No virtual-knot refinement, no irregular or missing tests in the sections read.
evidence_quotes: Sec. 3.1: "The SSM encoder is a stack of SSMs layers, each consisting of an SSM block followed by an MLP, see Figure 1b."
Sec. 3.1: "By adjusting $\Delta_{E}$ , the SSM can produce similar representations, irrespective of the sampling rate."
App. B.1 (Eq. 19): "for a sampling interval $\Delta>0$ , the continuous input is replaced by the piecewise-constant reconstruction"

App. B.1: "These operations act independently at each time step and therefore do not introduce additional temporal discretization error. They may, however, amplify or attenuate the mismatch produced by the SSM state."
App. B.1 (after Eq. 54): "Therefore, additional layers affect the prefactor of the equivariance error, but not its first-order dependence on the sampling interval."
Sec. 4: "hence the encoder representation is approximately invariant to the sampling rate and bound by the approximation error determined by the ZOH approximation in the SSM."
papers.reported_numbers: No HAR, EigenWorms, SC or PDM numbers (forecasting benchmarks only: GIFT-Eval, ETT). An ablation reports that removing time noise changes MASE from 0.725 to 0.740.
papers.notes: Prop. B.3 and Eqs 49-54 must be cited as EXISTING ODE/ZOH error inequalities (first order in max Delta). FlowState's own multi-layer remark treats later-layer inputs u_{l,Delta}(t) as continuous trajectories, yet in practice the per-step MLP outputs are re-held by ZOH for the next SSM layer. That is exactly where per-observation nonlinearities make the representation grid-dependent even for a refined identical path. FlowState bounds this at O(Delta) but never claims zero. N2's counterexample should target exactly this; the 'no additional discretization error' sentence is the one to scrutinize.

papers.title: Scalable Event-by-event Processing of Neuromorphic Sensory Signals With Deep State-Space Models
papers.sections_read: Abstract; 1 Introduction; 2 Related work; 3.1 S5 background (ZOH Eq. 7); 3.2 discretization on irregular event streams (Eqs 12-19), input normalization, parallelization, event-pooling; start of 4 Experiments
papers.mechanism: S5 applied event by event. The input is modelled as a sum of Dirac impulses at event times, so the state update is exp(Lambda delta Delta_k) x_{k-1} + B-bar u_k, with B-bar independent of Delta_k (event-time-independent normalization). Event pooling after each SSM layer forwards only every p-th state (averaging over p consecutive events) to C x and the following GLU/GELU nonlinearities.
papers.input_reconstruction: A Dirac impulse train (sum of delta(t - t_m) u_m). Under that model the linear update is exact.
papers.where_nonlinearity_evaluated: Per event in the first layer, and per pooled group of p events (index or event-count based, not physical time) in deeper layers.
papers.time_handling: Physical Delta_k = t_k - t_{k-1} in the transition, plus a learnable timescale delta.
papers.invariance_claim: None regarding sampling or grid invariance. The claims concern scalability and asynchronous integration.
papers.grid_changes_tested: None. The data are native irregular event streams (SHD, SSC, DVS128).
evidence_quotes: Sec. 3.2: "$\displaystyle\mathbf{u}(t)=\sum_{m=0}^{M}\delta\left(t-t_{m}\right)\mathbf{u}_{m}\,.$"
Sec. 3.2: "The normalization factor of an event should not depend on the relative timings of other asynchronous events."

Sec. 3.2 (Event-pooling): "Hence, $M$ inputs $\mathbf{u}_{m}$ are integrated into the state-space $\mathbf{x}$ , but only a subsampled sequence of length $M/p$ is forwarded to the linear transformation $\mathbf{\overline{C}}\mathbf{x}$ ."
Sec. 3.1: "A non-linear multiplicative interaction similar to the GLU activation (Dauphin et al., 2017) is applied to the SSM output"
papers.reported_numbers: Spiking Speech Commands: 88.4% (+7.7 points over the prior state of the art, per the abstract). No HAR/EW/SC-resolution/PDM numbers.
papers.notes: Exact integration here holds for impulse inputs, not for FOH paths. Inserting zero-valued virtual events would leave the linear state unchanged, but the per-event and event-count pooling nonlinearities break grid invariance. The multirate pooling is index-based.

papers.title: Hierarchical State Space Models for Continuous Sequence-to-Sequence Modeling (HiSS)

papers.title: It's Raw! Audio Generation with State-Space Models (SaShiMi)

papers.title: Efficiently Scanning and Resampling Spatio-Temporal Tasks with Irregular Observations

papers.title: Rough Transformers: Lightweight and Continuous Time Series Modelling through Signature Patching
papers.arxiv_or_venue: arXiv 2405.20799v3 [stat.ML], 11 Jan 2025; venue not verified in fetched text
papers.sections_read: Abstract; 1 Introduction; 2 background (signature, reparametrization invariance Eq. 7); 3 Rough Transformers (Eq. 8 multi-view signature, Eqs 9-10); 3.1 advantages incl. Prop. 3.1; 4.1-4.3 experiments (HR Table 1, UEA Table 2, Table 4, 50% drop Table 5); App. G drop tables 15-16
papers.mechanism: Observations are linearly interpolated into a path X-tilde. At a fixed set of time points t_k in T, the model computes multi-view signatures: global S(X)_{0,t_k} and local S(X)_{t_{k-1},t_k}, exact iterated integrals of the piecewise-linear path. A Transformer (multi-view attention) and an MLP run on this fixed-length sequence.
papers.input_reconstruction: Piecewise-linear interpolation, with EXACT signatures computed in closed form for piecewise-linear paths (Appendix A).
papers.where_nonlinearity_evaluated: Only on the fixed set of time points T, whose length is independent of the number of input samples (attention and MLP on signature features). The signature itself is a fixed nonlinear but exact functional of the path.
papers.time_handling: A fixed grid of signature window endpoints. Time can be added as a channel. Signatures are reparametrization-invariant.
papers.invariance_claim: APPROXIMATE robustness: Prop. 3.1 states T(X) ≈ T(X') for samplings of X-hat and X-hat∘gamma, via exact reparametrization invariance of signatures and continuity of attention and MLP. There is no explicit exact knot-refinement theorem and no separation of lossless from lossy grid change.
papers.grid_changes_tested: Random point drops of 30/50/70/85% (lossy missing data). Irregular sampling via drops. No lossless virtual-knot refinement test and no systematic downsampling-versus-aliasing study.
evidence_quotes: Sec. 3: "To project a discretized time-series $\mathbf{X}\in\mathcal{D}$ to a continuous-time object, let $\tilde{X}$ denote the piecewise-linear interpolation of $\mathbf{X}$ ."

Sec. 3.1: "The bounds of these integrals are a fixed set of time points, meaning that the sequence length of the multi-view attention mechanism is fixed and independent of the sequence length of input samples."

Prop. 3.1: "Suppose $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{X}^{\prime}$ are samplings of $\widehat{X}$ and $\widehat{X}\circ\gamma$ , respectively. Then $\mathbb{T}(\mathbf{X})\approx\mathbb{T}(\mathbf{X}^{\prime})$ ."
Sec. 3: "the local component as a type of convolutional filter that is invariant to the sampling rate of the signal."
papers.reported_numbers: EigenWorms (70/15/15 re-split): RFormer 90.3 ± 0.1. The Transformer runs out of memory. Baselines copied from Walker et al.: LRU 87.8, S5 81.1, S6 85.0, Mamba 70.9, NCDE 75.0, NRDE 83.9, LogNCDE 85.6. EW under drops (Table 15): 90.24 full, 87.86 at 30%, 87.69 at 50%, 83.35 at 70%, 82.74 at 85% (Transformer 72.45 at 85%). Table 5, 50% drop: EW 87.69, GRU 35.90, ODE-RNN 37.61, NRDE 60.68. HR RMSE: 2.66 ± 0.21 full, 2.96 at 50% drop (NRDE 2.97 as reported by Morrill et al.). Signature precompute: EigenWorms 1.11 s train / 0.19 s val.
papers.notes: Outside the SSM angle, but the most important non-SSM precedent for N2's central claim. It pairs an exact path-integral stem on a piecewise-linear reconstruction with nonlinearities only on a fixed time grid. Signatures of a piecewise-linear path are unchanged when collinear knots are inserted (Chen/reparametrization), so exact virtual-knot invariance of the stem is a known property here, even though the paper states only '≈'. The paper does not say whether T is fixed in physical time or tied to the index grid. TIDES (2605.09742) reports RFormer failing at unseen drop rates because 'its fixed signature window count [is] baked into positional encodings'. N2 must include RFormer (or fixed-grid signature + SSM/Transformer) as a near-work baseline, and must frame its novelty as a linear-SSM stem with exact FOH plus a fixed physical clock, with an explicit theorem and a separation of refinement, downsampling and missing data.

papers.title: Log Neural Controlled Differential Equations: The Lie Brackets Make a Difference
papers.arxiv_or_venue: arXiv 2402.18512v4 (23 Oct 2025); venue not verified in fetched text
papers.sections_read: Sec 2 background on NRDEs / Log-ODE method (Eqs around 21-22); Sec 3 Log-NCDE construction (depth-1 equivalence); Sec 4 toy/UEA setup (interval = 4 observations); Table 1 UEA results; Table 2 memory/time; App. dataset/hyperparameter notes (grep-level)
papers.mechanism: The Log-ODE method: on each interval [r_i, r_{i+1}], the CDE is replaced by an autonomous ODE driven by the depth-N truncated log-signature of the (linearly interpolated) control, with a vector field built from Lie brackets of f_theta. The ODE is solved numerically on each interval.
papers.input_reconstruction: Linear interpolation of the data, with a log-signature over each interval (exact for the piecewise-linear path).
papers.where_nonlinearity_evaluated: Continuously, inside a numerical ODE solver, on each interval. The vector field's log-signature term is constant per interval. The intervals are defined by observation counts (e.g. 4 observations), not by a fixed physical clock.
papers.time_handling: Time as a channel of the control path. Interval endpoints r_i are index-based in the experiments reported.
papers.invariance_claim: None about sampling or refinement in the sections read.
papers.grid_changes_tested: None in the sections read (the UEA sets are regular; duplicated EW series were removed).
evidence_quotes: Sec. 2: "Given a set of intervals $\{[r_{i},r_{i+1}]\}_{i=0}^{m-1}$ satisfying $t_{0}=r_{0}<\ldots<r_{m}=t_{n}$ , the Log-ODE method replaces a CDE with an ODE on each interval."
Sec. 4: "NRDE and Log-NCDE take $r_{i+1}-r_{i}$ to be $4$ observations and the signature truncation depth $N$ to be $2$ ."
Sec. 3: "the approach of NCDEs, NRDEs, and Log-NCDEs coincide when using a depth $-1$ Log-ODE approximation (Morrill et al., 2021)."
papers.reported_numbers: UEA EigenWorms (5 splits, 23 duplicated series removed): LRU 87.8 ± 2.8, S5 81.1 ± 3.7, S6 85.0 ± 16.1, Mamba 70.9 ± 15.8, NCDE 75.0 ± 3.9, NRDE 83.9 ± 7.3, Log-NCDE 85.6 ± 5.1. Average GPU memory / run time: Log-NCDE 1,999.67 MB / 2,128 s; S5 2,815 MB / 245 s.
papers.notes: Outside the SSM angle. Relevant because NRDE/Log-NCDE also split an exact per-interval path summary from the nonlinear dynamics, but the intervals are index-based and the nonlinear part is integrated continuously. The paper makes no refinement-invariance claim.

papers.title: TIDES: Implicit Time-Awareness in Selective State Space Models
papers.sections_read: Abstract; 1 Introduction; 2.1-2.2 continuous-time SSM / S5; 3 method (skimmed); 5 results incl. UEA table and 5.3 random drop; 6 related work and design-principle paragraph; App. B.1 ZOH; App. F random drop details; block definition (GELU/GLU)
papers.mechanism: A selective SSM in which input dependence is placed on Re(Lambda), B and C (low-rank projections of the current token) instead of on Delta. Delta stays the physical elapsed time via ZOH or bilinear discretization. The block is BN, then SSM, GELU, GLU, plus a residual.
papers.input_reconstruction: ZOH (input held constant on [t_k, t_{k+1})).
papers.where_nonlinearity_evaluated: At every observation (input-dependent decay, B and C per token, plus GELU/GLU per token).
papers.time_handling: Physical Delta_k = t_{k+1} - t_k enters only through the discretization.
papers.invariance_claim: A qualitative claim of 'faithful physical-time semantics' and extrapolation to out-of-distribution Delta or sampling density, shown empirically (Fading Flash; EW random drop). No exactness or refinement claim.
papers.grid_changes_tested: Random drop on EigenWorms (train at drop rate 0.5, test at 0.1-0.9, original timestamps kept) and out-of-distribution Delta on a synthetic task. No lossless refinement.
evidence_quotes: Abstract: "we propose TIDES, a selective SSM variant that reconciles selective and continuous architectures by moving input-dependence off the step size and onto the diagonal state matrix."
Sec. 6: "The physical sampling interval $\Delta_{k}$ should enter the model only through the rule that converts the continuous-time generator into a discrete recurrence"
App. B.1: "Assuming the input $u(t)$ is held constant on $[t_{k},t_{k+1})$ at value $u_{k}$ , the exact solution of (8) is"
Sec. 5.3: "RFormer fails analogously, with its fixed signature window count baked into positional encodings."
papers.reported_numbers: UEA EigenWorms: TIDES 85.7 ± 4.0 (same table: RFormer 90.3 ± 0.1, LRU 87.8, Log-NCDE 85.6). EW random drop (~30k parameters, trained at r = 0.5): TIDES mean accuracy 0.739, flat across r_test in {0.1, ..., 0.9}. Mamba_S falls from ~0.7 to ~0.4 at r_test = 0.9. S5 and TIDES_Lambda stay near chance.
papers.notes: The design principle 'keep discretization and expressivity separate' is conceptually adjacent to N2's separation principle. N2 should cite it and distinguish itself: TIDES still performs input-dependent (nonlinear) updates at every observation, so its representation is grid-dependent under knot refinement. Its random-drop test measures missing data, not lossless refinement.

papers.title: Efficient State Space Model via Fast Tensor Convolution and Block Diagonalization (eSSM)
papers.sections_read: Sec. 5.6 zero-shot raw speech classification (Table 3); dataset appendix (SC description)
papers.mechanism: A multi-input multi-output SSM with block diagonalization and FFT convolution. For resolution change, Delta is doubled at test time (16 to 8 kHz).
papers.input_reconstruction: None beyond the discretization rule (not specified in the section read).
papers.where_nonlinearity_evaluated: At every sample (standard deep SSM blocks).
papers.time_handling: dt-only rescaling.
papers.invariance_claim: Empirical zero-shot generalization only.
papers.grid_changes_tested: Real downsampling 16 to 8 kHz (SC10).
evidence_quotes: Sec. 5.6: "we rescale the time step $\Delta$ in the pre-trained model to twice the original value and all other model parameters remain unchanged."
papers.reported_numbers: Speech Commands 10-class (Table 3; MFCC / raw 16 kHz / zero-shot raw 8 kHz): S4 93.96 / 98.32 / 96.30; eSSM 94.46 / 97.59 / 94.23; CKConv 95.3 / 71.66 / 65.96; NRDE 89.8 / 16.49 / 15.12; Performer 80.85 / 30.77 / 30.68; ExpRNN 82.13 / 11.6 / 10.8. Mostly copied from the S4 paper's table.

papers.title: PASS: Path-selective State Space Model for Event-based Recognition
papers.sections_read: Abstract; 1 Introduction; 4.1 event sampling and frame aggregation (skimmed); 5.2.2 inference-frequency generalization
papers.mechanism: Events are aggregated into frames, and a learned path-selective scan selects a fixed number of frames, with an MSG loss against redundancy. A VideoMamba backbone follows.
papers.input_reconstruction: Event frames (time windows or event counts) plus learned selection. No path integration.
papers.where_nonlinearity_evaluated: At every selected frame or token.
papers.time_handling: Learned selection to a fixed number of frames.
papers.invariance_claim: Empirical robustness across inference frequencies.
papers.grid_changes_tested: Train at 20, 60 or 100 Hz and test at 20-100 Hz.
evidence_quotes: Sec. 1: "the varying sampling frequencies hinder the generalization of SSM during inference, as empirically verified in Tab. 5."
Sec. 5.2.2: "with a maximum performance drop of only 8.62% when our PASS model trained at 60 Hz and evaluated at 100 Hz."
papers.reported_numbers: PAF: maximum drop 8.62% (train 60 Hz, test 100 Hz). Baseline 'Time Windows' drops of -18.96, -20.69 and -29.32%.
papers.notes: Shows that selective SSMs such as Mamba do not generalize across frequencies by themselves. Low overlap.

papers.title: Neuromorphic Keyword Spotting with Pulse Density Modulation MEMS Microphones
papers.sections_read: Abstract; Introduction; Method (network topology); Experiments on oversampling ratio and sparsity (Fig. 2, Table 2); conclusion
papers.mechanism: PDM bits are fed directly into a 1D convolutional spiking network (ParaLIF-D). The first conv layer's kernel (3α) and stride (⌊3α/2⌋) scale with the oversampling ratio α, so later layers run at a roughly fixed physical rate. A separate model is trained per OSR.
papers.input_reconstruction: None (raw PDM bits).
papers.where_nonlinearity_evaluated: Spiking neurons at every strided output of layer 1 (a rate normalized by α) and at later layers.
papers.time_handling: Rate normalization is hard-coded in the first-layer stride. No continuous-time model.
papers.invariance_claim: None. Models are trained per OSR.
papers.grid_changes_tested: OSR 1-64, each trained separately.
evidence_quotes: Sec. 2: "Layer 1: 128 ParaLIF-D neurons, 1D convolution, kernel size of $3*\alpha$ , stride of $\lfloor 3*\alpha/2\rfloor$ , where $\alpha$ is the oversampling ratio."

Sec. 4: "changing the oversampling ratio has minimal impact on the network architecture, thanks to its inherent flexibility. Specifically, only the kernel size and stride of the first layer are adjusted accordingly."
papers.reported_numbers: GSC (35 classes) end-to-end from PDM: best 91.54 ± 0.23%. By OSR: 70.44 ± 0.30% at OSR 1, 81.55 ± 0.13% at OSR 2, 86.52 ± 0.17% at OSR 4. The exact OSR of the 91.54% result was not confirmed in the text read (the largest network is 210k parameters at OSR 64). Spike rate 122k/s at 16 kHz versus 206k/s at 1,024 kHz.
papers.notes: A PDM calibration point, and the prior work that 2608.28472 improves on. A stride proportional to OSR is a hand-coded fixed-clock stem, but it is learned per rate.

papers.title: Hierarchical temporal receptive windows and zero-shot timescale generalization in biologically constrained scale-invariant deep networks

papers.mechanism: Scale-invariant SITH-RNN built on Laplace-domain time cells, with a diagonal decay exp(-s Delta) analogous to a diagonal SSM.
papers.input_reconstruction: Not determined.
papers.where_nonlinearity_evaluated: Not determined (recurrent network).
papers.time_handling: Log-spaced time constants (scale invariance).
papers.invariance_claim: Zero-shot generalization to time-RESCALED sequences (dilation up to 3^6). This concerns stretching the signal, not changing the grid for the same signal.
papers.grid_changes_tested: Time rescaling of the stimulus.
evidence_quotes: Abstract: "the scale-invariant SITH-RNN learned faster with orders-of-magnitude fewer parameters, and generalized zero-shot to out-of-distribution timescales."
papers.reported_numbers: Not extracted (synthetic hierarchical language task).
